newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMANY'S KOHL FACES SUMMITS WEAKER THAN EVER BEFORE.
newsitem.headline: GERMANY'S KOHL FACES SUMMITS WEAKER THAN EVER BEFORE.

text.p: It used to be that Helmut Kohl dominated any international summit he attended. The veteran chancellor towered over his partners physically and politically and Germany's word was solid and dependable.
Not any more.
Kohl, the doyen of almost any international gathering these days, approaches three summits in the next two weeks looking weaker than at any time in his 14 years in office.

He will meet French President Jacques Chirac and his new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin at a bilateral session in Poitiers on June 13, attend the European Union's Amsterdam summit on June 16-17 and travel to Denver for the June 20-22 meeting of the G7 industrialised nations.

European monetary union (EMU), meant to be the crowning of the Christian Democrat (CDU) chancellor's long career, is now in serious trouble because the chancellor has failed to get Bonn's economic house in order for it.
Unemployment is at post-war record levels around 4.2 million and tax revenues regularly fall short of target.

Bonn's budget gaps are so huge -- now around 20 billion marks ($12 billion) -- that Bonn has begun to flirt with some of the same "creative accounting" it has long chided Italy or France for using to qualify for the euro.
Kohl's centre-right coalition government is in crisis and his authority, once massive enough to stifle all dissent, is sliding amid the unfamiliar discord of real debate in the ranks.

A newspaper on Monday quoted coalition sources as saying the chancellor threatened to resign several times last week when the government was unable to agree on measures to plug holes in the budget. A government spokesman had no immediate comment on the report.

Policy declarations once seen as visionary -- like Kohl's insistence that Germany will meet both the timetable and the criteria for the single currency -- now look more and more like evidence that he is out of touch with reality.
"I have linked part of my political thinking for decades -- and now my political existence -- with the idea that this goal must be reached," Kohl, 67, said on Sunday.
The chancellor has bounced back so often in the past that he can't be written off for a September 1998 general election, which he has pledged to fight to ensure his European vision becomes reality.

But even if it does, it won't be the way he wanted it. EMU was supposed to be part of a grander European integration drive including a political union to harmonise economic, social and foreign policies across the 15-member bloc.

The monetary union was supposed to keep member economies locked within a "stability pact" that ensure participants keep their budget deficits at or below three percent of gross domestic product and overall debt below 60 percent of GDP.
But Bonn, the plan's staunchest defender, now looks set to miss the criteria because it failed to adjust properly after reaching Kohl's other dream, German unification.
"The chancellor will simply have to give up his earlier goals and he's already doing this across a broad front," said ARD television commentator Rolf-Dieter Krause.
"He said before Maastricht (in 1991) there would only be a monetary union if there was a roughly equivalent political union. This was not reached in Maastricht.
"Instead they agreed to call another intergovernmental conference from 1996. This will be concluded in Amsterdam in a few days and it won't produce a political union either.

"Kohl always used to say criteria took precedence over the schedule. On Tuesday, he said the schedule is most important. This government is not reaching its own goals any more. So he will have to weaken the criteria.
"The idea that the Germans were a bulwark of stability for the euro - you can bury that idea now."
The balance of power among Kohl's partners in the EU and the G7 is also changing, and not necesssarily to his advantage.

With left-leaning prime ministers in two key EU countries -- Tony Blair in Britain and Lionel Jospin in France -- pressure has been building within the EU for the Maastricht treaty to include a special chapter on job creation.

The Kohl government has long opposed any Europe-wide drive to boost jobs, saying this must remain a preserve of national policy, but has become isolated on the issue at the intergovernmental conference and may have to make concessions.
In the G7, Blair has linked up with U.S. President Bill Clinton to push the idea of a jobs initiative within the club of rich industrialised states.
